lead: Fly-by-wire (FBW) replaces the mechanical link between cockpit and surface with wires, sensors and computers. The pilot moves a sidestick or column; gyros, accelerometers and air data measure the aircraft; redundant flight control computers use control laws to command hydraulic or electro-hydrostatic actuators. Fly-by-light (FBL) keeps the same chain but carries the signals over optical fibre. FBW is used on modern airliners and fighters because it saves weight, removes rigging and friction, and allows envelope protection and relaxed static stability.
prereq: You need: the chapter on powered flight controls for powered actuation and the chapter on Q-feel and servo tabs for artificial feel.

blocks.text: In a mechanical system the pilot's hand supplies the command and the rod or cable carries it. In FBW the command becomes an electrical signal. A sidestick or column has position sensors; rate gyros measure body angular rates p, q and r (roll, pitch and yaw rates in degrees per second); accelerometers measure normal acceleration n<sub>z</sub> in g; air data gives airspeed V, dynamic pressure q̄ in Pa (written with a bar so it is not confused with the pitch rate q) and angle of attack α. These signals enter the flight control computer (FCC). The pilot never pushes the surface directly; the FCC decides how much surface deflection gives the commanded motion.

items: Pilot input: sidestick position gives a demand, for example a pitch rate in degrees per second.
Sensors: gyros, accelerometers and air data measure the actual motion and air state.
FCC: three or four independent lanes compute the same command; a voter compares lanes and rejects a disagreeing lane.
Actuator: the FCC sends a command to a servo actuator, usually powered by hydraulic pressure; an electro-hydrostatic actuator has its own electric pump.
Surface: the actuator moves the aileron, elevator or rudder; the resulting motion is fed back by the sensors.

blocks.text: A control law is the formula or table that turns pilot and sensor inputs into actuator commands. A rate command law commands pitch rate, roll rate or yaw rate; the FCC compares commanded rate with measured rate and drives the surface until the error is small. For pitch, the C* (“C-star”) law blends pitch rate and normal acceleration: at low speed the pitch-rate part dominates, so it feels like a rate command; at high speed the normal-acceleration part dominates, so it feels like a load-factor (g) command. This gives consistent handling across the flight envelope.

items: Normal mode (normal law on Airbus types): all protections active: stall, overspeed, bank and load-factor limits.
Alternate mode: some protections lost; control laws simplified.
Direct mode: pilot command goes to the actuator with minimal feedback; no envelope protection.

blocks.text: FBW saves weight by deleting cables, pulleys, turnbuckles and rigging. It removes friction and backlash. The FCC can add envelope protection, carefree handling, gust alleviation and relaxed static stability, which allows a smaller tail. The cost is dependence on electric power, computers and validated software; lightning and electromagnetic interference (EMI) need protection.

Early FBW was analog. Digital FBW samples signals and runs software, so it can self-check, schedule gains by software, run built-in test (BIT), and grow by software change. Redundancy is by lanes, not by making one lane perfect. With three lanes, two good lanes outvote one bad lane. After that first failure only two remain, and two lanes that disagree cannot tell which one is wrong, so the system can only disconnect or drop to a backup. With four lanes a second failure can still be outvoted. The worked example puts numbers on this.

blocks.where: p is the failure probability of one lane in one flight hour; k is the number of independent lanes.

blocks.text: P(m or more of n fail) = Σ<sub>k=m…n</sub> C(n, k) p<sup>k</sup> (1 − p)<sup>n−k</sup> ≈ C(n, m) p<sup>m</sup>
blocks.where: C(n, k) is the number of ways to choose k lanes out of n; the approximation holds when p is small. Majority voting in a triplex is lost when m = 2 of n = 3 lanes fail.

blocks.text: Fly-by-light replaces the copper signal wires with optical fibre. It is immune to EMI, has no ground loops, cannot cause a spark at a fuel tank, is light and has high bandwidth. Problems are mechanical: fibre has a minimum bending radius, every connector loses optical power, and the optical power budget must close. FBL still uses hydraulic or electric power at the actuator.

Below, a table: one lane 1 times 10 to the minus 4; triplex all fail 1 times 10 to the minus 12; triplex majority lost 3 times 10 to the minus 8; quadruplex majority lost 4 times 10 to the minus 12.

examples.question: A digital FBW computer has independent lanes, each failing with probability p = 1 × 10⁻⁴ in a flight hour. (a) For three lanes, find the probability that all three fail in one hour. (b) Majority voting needs two good lanes out of three. Find the probability of losing the majority (two or more lanes failed). (c) For four lanes, find the probability that three or more fail. Compare each with a target of 1 × 10⁻⁹ per hour.

code.code:
from math import comb

p = 1e-4   # failure probability of one lane in one flight hour

def at_least(m, n):
    """probability that m or more of n independent lanes fail"""
    return sum(comb(n, k) * p**k * (1 - p)**(n - k) for k in range(m, n + 1))

print(f"triplex, all 3 fail:      {p**3:.2e}")
print(f"triplex, 2 or more fail:  {at_least(2, 3):.2e}")
print(f"quadruplex, 3 or more:    {at_least(3, 4):.2e}")

steps: Independence means the probabilities multiply. Let p = 1 × 10⁻⁴.
(b) Two or more of three fail: P = C(3,2) p² (1 − p) + p³ = 3 × 10⁻⁸ × 0.9999 + 10⁻¹² = 3.00 × 10⁻⁸ per hour.
(c) Three or more of four fail: P = C(4,3) p³ (1 − p) + p⁴ = 4 × 10⁻¹² × 0.9999 + 10⁻¹⁶ = 4.00 × 10⁻¹² per hour.

Compare with 1 × 10⁻⁹: the triplex all-fail value (10⁻¹²) passes, but the triplex loses its majority 30 times more often than the target. The quadruplex keeps a voting majority to 4 × 10⁻¹², which passes. This is why many FBW computers are quadruplex, or triplex with a dissimilar backup.

triplex, all 3 fail:      1.00e-12
triplex, 2 or more fail:  3.00e-08
quadruplex, 3 or more:    4.00e-12
examples.answer: (a) 1.00 × 10⁻¹² per hour; (b) 3.00 × 10⁻⁸ per hour, which misses a 10⁻⁹ target; (c) 4.00 × 10⁻¹² per hour, which meets it.

traps: FBW removes the mechanical linkage, not hydraulic power; actuators still need hydraulic or electric power.
Artificial feel remains: sidestick springs and Q-feel create stick force, not airload feedback through cables.
Saying analog FBW had no computer. Analog FBW used analog computers; what digital FBW adds is sampling, software (which must be validated), built-in test and gain scheduling in software.
Fly-by-light is not wireless: optical fibre carries signals, while actuator power still comes by wire or hydraulic line.
Voting lanes improve availability; the usual design answer is not one perfect lane but independent lanes with comparison and isolation.

quiz.a: It replaces the mechanical linkage between cockpit and surface with electrical signals, sensors, computers and actuators; hydraulic power may remain.

quiz.q: Why does a FBW aircraft still need artificial feel?
quiz.a: The pilot no longer feels airloads through a mechanical link, so springs or a Q-feel unit must create a stick force. A sidestick spring gives force that rises with deflection only; Q-feel also makes it rise with speed.

quiz.q: A lane fails at 2 × 10⁻⁵ per hour. For three independent lanes find the probability that all three fail and the probability that two or more fail.
quiz.a: All three: (2 × 10⁻⁵)³ = 8 × 10⁻¹⁵ per hour. Two or more: about 3p² = 3 × 4 × 10⁻¹⁰ = 1.2 × 10⁻⁹ per hour.

quiz.q: Why are three or four lanes used instead of one highly reliable lane?
quiz.a: Independent lanes with voting isolate a failed lane and prevent a single fault from commanding the surface. The probability of all k lanes failing falls as p<sup>k</sup>; a common software fault or a power loss can still take every lane, so dissimilarity and separate power supplies are added.

quiz.q: Name two normal-mode protections and state what direct mode gives up.
quiz.a: Stall and overspeed protection, or bank and load-factor limits. Direct mode gives up envelope protection and much feedback; pilot command goes more directly to the actuator.

quiz.q: Give two reasons fly-by-light suits routing near fuel tanks and two optical problems.
quiz.a: Fibre carries light, not current, so a damaged fibre cannot spark, and it puts no conducting path into the tank for lightning current. Problems: minimum bend radius and the optical power lost at each connector; the optical power budget must close.

quiz.q: State two advantages of digital over analog FBW.
quiz.a: Self-checking and built-in test; software gain scheduling. Software growth and fault isolation are also easier.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, FBW design is tied to systems safety and software assurance; FBL flies in production on the Kawasaki P-1 maritime patrol aircraft and on research aircraft, because of EMI and fuel-tank safety. Search next for 'fly-by-light optical power budget', 'dissimilar redundancy flight control' and 'C* control law'. Newer curricula connect this chapter to integrated modular avionics and model-based software validation.
